learningJourney.title: What are the Four Core Algorithm Patterns

explanation.foundation: Most brute-force sequence and optimization algorithms fail at scale because they re-examine identical ranges (`O(n^2)`) or recompute identical subproblems (`O(2^n)`). These four patterns eliminate redundant work by exploiting structural invariants:
explanation.core:
- **Two Pointers**: On sorted or partitioned data, `left` and `right` move monotonically, pruning `O(n^2)` pairs to `O(n)` in `O(1)` space.
- **Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's)**: Advancing `slow` by `+1` and `fast` by `+2` detects cycles and midpoints in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space.
- **Sliding Window**: Expands `right` to include state and shrinks `left` only when a monotonic invariant breaks (`O(n)` amortized).
- **Dynamic Programming (DP)**: Caches overlapping subproblems (`dp[i]` or `dp[i][j]`) via memoization or bottom-up tabulation.

ideas.description: Scanning a full timestamp log on every request degraded to O(n) under 50k RPS bursts. A Sliding Window deque (evicting `< now - 60s` from `left` while pushing `now` at `right`) reduced per-request amortized work to O(1) (<0.3 ms p99).

learningJourney.title: How to implement Sliding Window & 1D Compressed DP Safely

explanation.foundation: In **0/1 Knapsack** (`dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w - wt[i]])`), row `i` depends only on row `i-1` at smaller weights.

prerequisites.summary: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.
